A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Statistical Inference under Performativity, retaining the same RRM and prediction-powered inference framework. The main text, equations, figures, and complete Appendices A and B are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original simulations of confidence-region coverage and width, normality diagnostics, score-matching accuracy, and parameter sensitivity.

after.justification: The original simulations remain, and Appendix B.3 adds original semi-synthetic credit-scoring experiments reported in Figure A4.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the stated policy-perturbation estimator: v1 subtracts unnormalized sums, whereas v3 includes the respective 1/k and 1/n sample-mean factors. The RRM updates, score-matching objective, bias adjustment, and greedy PPI procedure otherwise remain. This establishes a formula correction, not that implementations or experiments were changed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic performative linear regression. V3 adds the GiveMeSomeCredit semi-synthetic credit-scoring task, using logistic regression and applicants strategically manipulating features. This substantially extends coverage to real applicant data, binary classification, and feature-distribution feedback.

E2.justification: The evaluated alternatives remain labeled-only inference with lambda = 0, full-weight PPI with lambda = 1, and greedy lambda selection. The added credit experiment reuses these alternatives. Newly discussed prior theoretical work is not added as an experimental baseline.

E3.justification: The original simulation settings and coverage/width metrics are retained. The added credit protocol treats the original dataset as the population for computing the stable point, constructs unlabeled features with Gaussian noise, and uses N = 18,000, five RRM steps, and labeled sample sizes from 10,000 to 18,000. These are settings for an additional experiment.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a case study examining whether the inference procedure maintains coverage and narrow intervals under strategic credit-scoring feedback. The existing regularization, sensitivity, and noise ablations, normality diagnostics, and Gaussian-versus-DNN score-estimation analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: V3 newly specifies 1,000 independent trajectories and averaging across their policies for the Figure 3 score-matching results. It also reports 100 independent trials for the added credit study. The original coverage experiments retain 1,000 trials and the same interval construction; no increase in their run counts is established.

E6.justification: Results in Figures 1–3 and A1–A3 are retained. New Figure A4 reports credit-scoring results: greedy lambda produces the narrowest intervals and approximately 0.92–0.98 coverage. Contrary to the accompanying blanket highest-coverage claim, lambda = 1 has slightly higher coverage at n = 10,000. These are additional results under a new setting.

T1.justification: V3 adds Theorem 3.6 and Appendix A.3, including explicit regularity, entropy, optimization, and model-richness assumptions, score-estimation bounds, and a proof bounding error in estimating the RRM Jacobian. Assumptions A.1 and A.5 strengthen positive definiteness to uniform lower bounds. Corollary 3.7 replaces boundedness of the entire parameter space with bounds on the initial and stable parameters, followed by a derivation of a feasible bound and an interval-rate comparison.

C1.justification: V1 broadly claims the first statistical inference framework under performativity. V3 acknowledges an earlier performative CLT and narrows the central novelty claim to a complete, data-driven inference framework for batch RRM. This materially revises the claimed firstness, while retaining the RRM CLT and performative PPI contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds an interpretation of improved interval-width rates relative to earlier RRM bounds, qualified by data dimension and omission of the bias adjustment. It also explains the on-policy data-collection difficulty motivating semi-synthetic evaluation and interprets the credit results as evidence of practical relevance. The limitation that stable-point inference remains bias-aware is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 supplies a dataset-access footnote, the logistic-regression setting, empirical-population construction, and Gaussian-noise generation of unlabeled features. Existing DNN architecture, SGD learning rate, and A100 hardware disclosures remain. The new case does not specify the exact strategic-response map, noise variance, or annotating-model training.

R1.justification: V3 adds substantive discussion of Cutler et al. (2024) and Bracale et al. (2024), including a dedicated inference-under-performativity paragraph. It positions its contribution around batch updates and data-driven covariance estimation in relation to earlier inference work, and adds a theoretical comparison with Perdomo et al. (2020). This substantially revises the nearest-prior-work positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and score-matching passages are rewritten, citations change to author-year style, and terminology and affiliation details are edited. Dedicated policy-perturbation and case-study subsections are inserted, shifting the existing PPI appendix from A.3 to A.4. The overall narrative and most existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: V3 adds the two-panel credit-scoring Figure A4. Existing Figures 1–3 and A1–A3 retain their graphical content and move with text reflow. Author affiliations move to first-page footnotes, while the basic single-column layout remains.

improvement.justification: V3 corrects the estimator normalization, more carefully delimits novelty, and supplies explicit policy-perturbation assumptions and error analysis where v1 largely assumed optimizer consistency. These improve clarity and technical support. The credit study adds useful evidence, but its implementation is incompletely specified, its highest-coverage claim has a plotted exception, and the new rate comparison insufficiently distinguishes finite-sample from asymptotic guarantees. The net improvement is therefore positive but qualified.
